title: Middle: Melanie, Discovery & Exorcism
content_html:
Jeanette and Melanie: First Love

Jeanette meets Melanie at church — Melanie is a new convert whom Jeanette brings into the congregation. Their relationship develops naturally from friendship into love: Jeanette describes it simply and tenderly, with none of the shame or crisis that the church will later impose. Winterson deliberately presents the relationship as innocent and joyful: "I loved her so much my stomach felt as though it were full of air." The simile makes love physical and immediate — it is a bodily sensation, not an intellectual concept. Winterson refuses to present Jeanette's sexuality as a problem to be solved or a sin to be repented.

The chapter title "Leviticus" is deeply ironic. In the Bible, Leviticus contains the laws governing sexual behaviour — including the passage (Leviticus 18:22) that many Christians cite to condemn homosexuality. By naming the chapter where Jeanette falls in love after the very book used to condemn her love, Winterson creates a structural irony that runs throughout the novel: the Bible that Jeanette has been raised on becomes the weapon used against her.

Key Fact

Winterson presents Jeanette and Melanie's relationship as natural and joyful — not sinful. The chapter title 'Leviticus' creates structural irony: the biblical book of sexual laws names the chapter where Jeanette discovers same-sex love.

Discovery and the Church's Reaction

When the church discovers Jeanette's relationship with Melanie, the response is swift and violent. The congregation does not discuss, counsel, or attempt to understand — it condemns. Jeanette is accused of harbouring "a demon" and of being under "the influence of the Devil." The language is significant: by framing Jeanette's love as demonic possession, the church denies Jeanette's agency. Her love is not something she has chosen or felt; it is an external force that has invaded her. This allows the church to 'save' her through exorcism without ever engaging with the reality of her identity.

The church's response reveals the community's fundamental inability to tolerate difference. As long as Jeanette conformed — preaching, evangelising, obeying — she was valued. The moment she diverged, she became not merely wrong but evil. Winterson shows how the binary worldview established in the early chapters ('friends and enemies') now turns against Jeanette: there is no category for a good person who happens to be gay. You are either righteous or demonic.

The Exorcism Scene

The exorcism is one of the novel's most powerful scenes. Jeanette is brought before the congregation, placed in a room, and subjected to prayer, fasting, and physical confinement. She is kept without food for days. The congregation prays over her, demanding that the 'demon' leave. Winterson describes the scene with characteristic understatement: "I couldn't understand what was happening. The hymns were too loud. The hands were too heavy." The short, simple sentences mirror Jeanette's disorientation. The repetition of "too" suggests overwhelming sensory assault — the exorcism is not spiritual healing but physical and psychological abuse.

After the exorcism, Jeanette is told she has been 'cured' and must repent. She agrees — not because she believes her love was wrong, but because she has no other option. Winterson makes clear that Jeanette's compliance is survival, not conversion. She tells us: "I miss God. I miss the company of someone utterly loyal." This extraordinary line reveals that Jeanette does not reject God — she rejects the church's interpretation of God. Her faith and her sexuality are not in conflict; it is the institution that creates the conflict.

Melanie's response to the church's condemnation contrasts sharply with Jeanette's. Melanie submits completely: she repents publicly, marries a man, and conforms to the church's expectations. Winterson uses Melanie as a foil to Jeanette. Where Jeanette ultimately refuses to deny who she is, Melanie chooses survival through conformity. Neither response is presented as morally superior — Winterson shows the impossible choice the church forces: be yourself and lose everything, or deny yourself and keep your community.

Key Fact

The exorcism is a pivotal scene: the church frames Jeanette's love as demonic possession, denying her agency. The short, fragmented sentences convey physical and psychological abuse. Jeanette's compliance is survival, not genuine repentance — she 'misses God' but rejects the church's interpretation.

The Orange Demon: A Key Symbol

During and after the exorcism, Jeanette imagines a conversation with a "small orange demon" who tells her: "Everyone has a demon... The demon you get depends on the life you lead." The orange demon is not evil — it is Jeanette's own identity, the part of herself that the church is trying to destroy. By making the 'demon' orange (the title fruit) and articulate, Winterson subverts the church's framing: what they call demonic is actually Jeanette's truest self. The orange demon says everyone has one — implying that identity itself is what the church fears and tries to control.
exam_tip_html: For the exorcism scene, analyse Winterson's sentence structure: "The short, declarative sentences — 'The hymns were too loud. The hands were too heavy.' — mirror Jeanette's disorientation under sensory assault. The repetition of 'too' conveys overwhelming force disguised as spiritual care. Winterson presents the exorcism not as healing but as institutional abuse."
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jeanette and Melanie's love is presented as natural and joyful — the chapter title 'Leviticus' creates structural irony.
  • The church frames Jeanette's sexuality as demonic possession, denying her agency and reducing identity to sin.
  • The exorcism scene uses short, fragmented sentences to convey physical and psychological abuse.
  • The orange demon represents Jeanette's authentic self — what the church calls 'demonic' is actually identity.

glossary_terms.definition: A comparison using 'like' or 'as' — love compared to a physical sensation, making the abstract emotion visceral.
Irony created by the structure of the text — the chapter titled after biblical sexual laws is where Jeanette discovers love.
The capacity to make choices on one's own behalf — calling Jeanette's love 'demonic' denies that she chose or owns it.
A character who contrasts with the protagonist — Melanie's submission highlights Jeanette's refusal to deny her identity.
A symbolic figure representing Jeanette's authentic self — what the church calls 'demonic' is actually her identity.
Behaviour causing physical, emotional, or psychological harm — the exorcism functions as abuse disguised as spiritual care.
